message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing pixels on screen, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 in consumer CPUs). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores (e.g., 1,000+ CUDA cores in an NVIDIA RTX card). |
| **Execution style** | Serial/low‑latency – each core can execute complex instructions with deep pipelines and sophisticated branch prediction. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – many cores perform the same operation on different data simultaneously; great for throughput. |
| **Clock speed** | Higher clock speeds (≈3–5 GHz) because fewer cores need to finish tasks quickly. | Lower clock speeds (≈1–1.5 GHz) because power budget is shared across many cores. |
| **Cache hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core to keep frequently accessed data close. | Smaller per‑core cache; relies on high memory bandwidth instead. |
| **Memory access patterns** | Random, unpredictable accesses typical of general software. | Coalesced, predictable accesses; thrives when many threads read/write contiguous memory. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set architecture (CISC) like x86, capable of many operations per cycle. | Simpler, often RISC‑style; optimized for arithmetic and vector operations. |
| **Typical workloads** | Operating system services, database queries, web servers, office applications, gaming logic. | Rendering frames, physics simulations, AI inference/training, scientific simulations, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power consumption** | Lower total power for a single core but higher per‑core power due to complexity. | High total power for the whole chip, but lower per‑core power; GPUs are built to run at high throughput within a thermal envelope. |

### Why the differences matter

* **Parallelism** – A GPU’s many cores excel when you have a task that can be split into thousands of identical sub‑tasks (e.g., processing every pixel in an image). A CPU’s few cores are better when tasks depend on each other or require complex branching.

* **Latency vs. throughput** – CPUs minimize latency (time to complete one task), while GPUs maximize throughput (total work done over time).

* **Software ecosystem** – CPUs run almost all operating systems and most software stacks. GPUs require specialized drivers and APIs (OpenGL, DirectX, Vulkan, CUDA, OpenCL) to harness their parallelism.

In short, CPUs are versatile “master chefs” that can handle a wide variety of tasks quickly, whereas GPUs are “assembly line workers” that can process many similar tasks in parallel very efficiently.
